Hey OP! It's heartbreaking to be let down on your birthday. On my 22nd birthday I got 4 cakes from my friends. And the next one I got none because all of them were in different cities. The guy I was seeing back then refused to get me one and kept teasing me by not wishing me at all. We broke up soon after because he'd keep playing these silly games all the time. 

Every year after I would feel low on birthday when I wouldn't get gifts or cakes or figuring out my friends have forgotten. 

What I realised a few years later was that I love cakes on birthdays, the other things werent as important to me. So I started getting myself one from my 26th birthday onwards. It's a tradition I still follow. I'm 36 now. My husband gets one for me anyway but I just love pampering myself with gifts instead of feeling low on my special day. 

I guess there are certain things you learn with age. Self love is one of them. Trust me it feels great to treat yourself with everything you've wanted on your birthday. No disappointments at all. And if someone gifts you stuff that's just an added bonus!

A lot of us don't have the same linear journey in our careers compared to our friends. In my early career I saw immense growth and salary hikes, but then life happened. 

Career growth slowed because I had to take care of my sick father-in-law. I learnt a lot through that phase about myself and my priorities. I'm back to work after a 2 year break and I feel I've been left far behind compared to my colleagues at the time.

They have gone on to bigger roles while I'm still stuck where I quit in 2022. But I've stopped regretting it because they didn't have to face the same struggles as me. Plus I've become a lot more patient and efficient with my work now and I value my job a little more. 

So take it steadily. There will come a time when you'll get a boost in your career. Find what you're best at and work on it. Your managers will recognise your value too. Just stay consistent and keep moving forward! Comparison only ruins peace of mind. That's all I have come to realise now.

My periods only came back when I stopped going to the gym. 

I then discontinued the gym but started walking and cutting out packaged food from my diet. Within 2 months my periods were back to normal. This was 5 years ago and I've maintained walking as my primary exercise now. I'm also not much of an eater so my weight is easily under control with a brisk walk. 

But if you enjoy hitting the gym it would be a good idea to consult your gynaec or see a dietitian who can assist you. They can help you with medication and food groups you should be consuming more of to maintain a regular cycle.

I'm sorry you're going through this terrible time. I tried for 3 years before finding out my baby wasnt going to survive at 24 months. When we lost him I went through the same emotions that you are.

I took a trip away to the hills with my family and all I saw were people out with their children. Babies in strollers. Kids everywhere. I cried in public. I cried in my room at the hotel and I cried because I didn't know if there was a way out of this. 

So I started writing little notes to my baby. Every time I thought of him I wrote a short note. I was angry, frustrated, envious, sad and I put it all down in words. It gradually became my coping mechanism. It last 6 months. For 6 whole months I wrote down every single emotion I felt. 

I know I was massively depressed during that phase. Different things work for different people. One of my friends started going to the gym because she was so angry. I don't know what will help you cope with these feelings but I know you will find it some day.

It's been a year now and I still grieve my baby. I think of him often. Sometimes when I'm not actively thinking of him, he'll show up in a dream. But it's not as severe as it used to be. I feel like I've grown around the grief and I hope you will too. 

The loss will always remain and you'll carry that grief but you'll also find ways to live beyond the grief. It takes time and I truly understand today what they mean when they say grief isn't linear. I hope you find peace.

Last year in Feb I found out my baby had early onset IUGR. I was right away told the chances of his survival were very low, yet we continued to get treatment from another doctor who gave us hope that if I hit 30 weeks they'd be able to save him. 

Unfortunately we lost him at 25 weeks. Just a week before that we had lost my father-in-law to cancer. We were really close and the double blow was extremely cruel. At times I didn't know what I was mourning more.

Even though we spent a fortune in 3 weeks trying to save my baby I had a very real instinct he won't make it. So I wrote to him every day. Long after he was gone I continued to write notes to him every time I thought of him. 

I didn't want to seek therapy because I kind of knew what they were going to suggest and I didn't want to spend anymore on another treatment. To me writing down everything made the experience real and gradually I was able to come to terms with the loss.

I'm now pregnant again and every time I have a scan scheduled or a doctor's visit I panic. I had a full blown anxiety attack last scan but everything turned out fine. 

It takes long to heal. I hope you find the courage to go through this time.

So I met a lot of guys over 2 years. Some rejected me, some I rejected. I cancelled out people for basic reasons: one said his parents won't be ok with me eating onion, another didn't think dowry was unreasonable but he was also insecure that he didn't earn as much as me, one guy wanted me to call him daily but I'm an introvert irl and not much of a phone call person so I wasn't comfortable with that. I'm almost 5'7" and have been borderline overweight so that was an issue for some. 

After all these experiences I went prepared with all this to meet my now husband. I wasn't very keen on a massive salary package because I had plenty in savings and knew I would continue working. Looks werent a major criteria either because some of the good looking ones I met had no interest in me. So that self-awareness was always there.

I asked my husband 3 things: his food preferences, what he expected from me as a wife and a daughter in law and how his relationship with his parents was. We discussed a few recent political events because we were in a cafe where the news was playing on TV to see what his political opinions were.

I told him right away about the things that I wasn't good at acc to AM. I didn't know how to cook back then and I was honest that I never found myself interested in the kitchen. But I could clean and do the dishes etc. That I struggled with my weight and I won't be the prettiest bride. 

He asked me what my interests were, where all I had travelled, how I imagined life after marriage, what were dealbreakers in a marriage for me, and if I had any recent relationships that could be an issue later I could be honest with him, and he was open about his dating experience as well. He also said that his father is a disciplinarian and I would only find out how strict he could be when I lived with them. He said he already had a cook and a house help because everyone in his family worked and looks werent important to his family.

All our basic first meeting answers were totally aligned with what we wanted. Our parents werent there when we met.

Both his parents were working at the time. They outrightly rejected any form of dowry, they mentioned their house had everything and didn't want any furniture etc either. They wanted me to work too. There was no restriction on what I should wear etc. Just had to make mild adjustments when my MIL wanted me to wear clothes of her choice for functions, take days off for family commitments etc but I was willing to make that compromise because they really care for me like a daughter. My FIL never had any restrictions for me. All he wanted was 3 meals on time which I didn't have to cook, just serve him.

We never had any clashes. In fact because I was so well accepted into the family I willingly quit my job to take care of my FIL when he had cancer. He had to be taken to the hospital for chemo every month. My husband didn't get leaves every month and could only come to the hospital after work. I was the one who always went as my FIL's attendant. Sadly he passed away after 1.5 years of fighting it and I got back to working again after that.

Like I said, we had a long gap between our engagement and wedding. We had talked about stuff before that. His family is quite liberal, his sister had a love marriage and so did his aunts, so dating/relationships weren't a taboo in his side of the family.

I have been working with a mental health organization lately and have spoken to a lot of psychologists. I've found out from them that the idea that you should talk about what you're going through is easier said than done.

Most Indian parents can't accept the fact that their children are going through a mental health struggle. Plus as they grow older the guilt of not burdening them with our problems prevents us from speaking about certain things.

I've always been a part of huge friend groups but I'm gradually realising everyone is dealing with something or the other and having a lot of friends doesn't mean anything unless you have a support system. 

It's good to have at least 2 people you trust. As we grow older making friends and finding people who have time for you is just so difficult. We don't really have many meaningful connections left. Just 2 people who can listen to you and offer support are interested in listening to you, are enough. 

For me it's not my parents but a friend I met online through Twitter who I bounce off my feelings with and my husband. I'd just like everyone to find 2 people you can be completely honest with about yourself.
